description: Daily consumption of high-polyphenol Cretan olive oil has been shown in clinical research to measurably reduce key inflammation markers — including CRP and IL-6 — with effects persisting even after stopping. The primary drivers are oleocanthal, which blocks the same COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes targeted by ibuprofen, and hydroxytyrosol, a potent antioxidant that neutralises harmful free radicals.

Making Cretan olive oil a daily habit — even just half a tablespoon — is linked in large-scale studies to a 15–30% lower risk of serious heart disease. It works through multiple pathways: oleic acid helps the body clear excess cholesterol, while its polyphenols reduce vascular inflammation and improve blood vessel function by increasing nitric oxide availability.

Studies show that drinking Cretan mountain tea daily for a month can measurably sharpen attention and reduce anxiety — in a gold-standard clinical trial of 155 older adults, a daily 950mg dose reduced attention errors and lowered state anxiety more effectively than Ginkgo biloba. The likely mechanism is a dual one: the tea's hydroxycinnamic acids and flavonoids increase blood flow to the prefrontal cortex acutely, and reduce anxiety over longer periods by slowing the breakdown of mood-regulating neurotransmitters.

Research suggests that a daily Sideritis extract can meaningfully support heart and metabolic health: in a randomised controlled trial of healthy adults taking 1500mg daily for four weeks, systolic blood pressure dropped by nearly 11 mmHg, resting heart rate fell, aerobic capacity improved, and blood markers of oxidative damage decreased significantly. The polyphenols — particularly verbascoside, which directly binds the NF-κB inflammation pathway — appear to protect blood vessels and liver cells from free-radical damage.

Studies show that daily purslane supplementation can dramatically reduce joint inflammation — in a gold-standard clinical trial of 86 people with rheumatoid arthritis, taking 1000mg daily for 12 weeks more than halved pain scores, cut swollen and tender joint counts by over 60%, and significantly reduced CRP and TNF-α. The mechanism centres on purslane's omega-3 fatty acids and kaempferol, which suppress the same inflammatory cytokine pathways that drive chronic joint and tissue inflammation throughout the body.

Studies show that purslane consistently improves blood fats and fasting blood sugar in people with type 2 diabetes: a meta-analysis of multiple randomised trials found significant reductions in fasting blood glucose (−15 mg/dL), triglycerides (−21 mg/dL), and LDL cholesterol, alongside a meaningful rise in protective HDL cholesterol. These effects are thought to stem from purslane's exceptionally high alpha-linolenic acid — the plant omega-3 that the body converts into EPA and DHA — along with polyphenols that reduce inflammatory stress on blood vessel walls.

Research suggests that purslane extract can meaningfully improve gut function: in a randomised controlled trial of 60 people with functional constipation, eight weeks of supplementation significantly increased bowel movement frequency, shortened colonic transit time from 44.5 to 33.7 hours, and improved overall digestive quality of life. The likely drivers are purslane's mucilaginous polysaccharides, which act as a gentle bulk-forming agent that speeds up the movement of food through the colon.

Research suggests that regular hard cheese consumption offers surprisingly broad protection against major diseases: a comprehensive umbrella review covering 47 health outcomes found that cheese consumers had 8% fewer cardiovascular events, 19% lower dementia risk, 10% fewer fractures, and 5% lower all-cause mortality across hundreds of prospective studies. These benefits are thought to arise despite the saturated fat content — driven by vitamin K2, which prevents calcium from accumulating in artery walls, bioactive peptides that reduce blood pressure, and calcium that supports bone and metabolic health.

Studies show that cheese specifically — as distinct from other dairy products — is consistently linked to lower cardiovascular disease and stroke risk across global populations: a 2025 analysis drawing on the UK Biobank and Chinese population cohorts, published in Nature Communications, found that cheese consumption was associated with a 3.7% lower cardiovascular disease risk and a 6% lower stroke risk in meta-analysis. Graviera, made from Cretan sheep and goat milk, provides the same bioactive compounds — vitamin K2, CLA, and antihypertensive peptides — thought to underlie this protection.

Laboratory research has identified probiotic bacteria native to traditional Graviera cheese with promising gut and cardiovascular properties: Lactobacillus plantarum strains isolated directly from Graviera adhered strongly to human gut epithelial cells, stimulated anti-inflammatory immune responses, and produced compounds that inhibit ACE — the same enzyme targeted by blood-pressure-lowering drugs. These findings are from laboratory cell experiments and have not yet been confirmed in human trials, but they point to Graviera's artisanal fermentation process as a source of potentially health-promoting live bacteria.

Research shows that applying thyme honey gel to the mouth during chemotherapy can meaningfully protect against one of treatment's most painful side effects: in a clinical trial of 110 breast cancer patients, using a thyme honey oral gel reduced the chance of developing moderate-to-severe mouth ulcers, shortened their duration by over three days, and delayed their onset — all with statistical significance. The protective effects are thought to stem from thyme honey's exceptionally high polyphenol content and thymol, which suppress the inflammatory cascade responsible for breaking down the mucosal lining of the mouth.

Animal research suggests that thyme honey can produce powerful metabolic and organ-protective effects: in diabetic rats, a combination of thyme honey and olive oil nearly halved elevated blood glucose (from 318 to 159 mg/dL within 30 days), normalised abnormal blood fats, and shielded the liver, pancreas, and kidneys from oxidative damage — with tissue structure recovering close to normal. Thyme honey's polyphenols, measured at 193 mg per 100g — among the highest recorded for any honey variety — appear to drive these antioxidant effects. These findings are from an animal model and have not yet been confirmed in human trials.

Laboratory research suggests that thyme honey has dual gut-protective properties: in bacterial experiments, it inhibited the biofilms of harmful bacteria — including Staphylococcus aureus by up to 80% and Acinetobacter baumannii by over 50% — while simultaneously stimulating the growth of the beneficial probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus and boosting its antioxidant capacity by nearly 66%. This combination of pathogen suppression and probiotic stimulation is the defining characteristic of a prebiotic. These effects have been demonstrated in laboratory conditions only and remain to be confirmed in human studies.

Laboratory research suggests that stamnagathi may support brain health by targeting two defining features of Alzheimer's disease simultaneously: in neuronal cell experiments, the extract reduced toxic tau protein, blocked the enzymes that drive its harmful hyperphosphorylation, and shifted the processing of the amyloid precursor protein away from the amyloid-producing pathway — addressing both the neurofibrillary tangle and amyloid plaque pathways that underlie the disease. These findings are from cell culture experiments only and have not yet been tested in animals or humans, but they point to stamnagathi's polyphenol profile as a potential neuroprotective agent.

Laboratory research suggests that stamnagathi has meaningful antioxidant and vascular-protective effects: an extract containing cichoric acid, caftaric acid, quercetin, and luteolin raised the master cellular antioxidant glutathione (GSH) and reduced free radicals in human endothelial cells — the cells lining blood vessels that are central to cardiovascular health. The extract showed strong radical scavenging activity (ABTS IC50 28 μg/mL) and a total polyphenol content of 117 mg per gram of dry extract. These effects were observed in cell culture experiments and have not yet been confirmed in human trials.

Research suggests that the traditional Cretan preparation of stamnagathi — boiling the leaves as a decoction — produces a potent antioxidant with properties unique to the Cretan species: scientists characterising the Cretan water decoction found it safe for human cells, significantly reduced cellular oxidative stress, and contains a sulfoconjugate sesquiterpene lactone that exists only in Cretan stamnagathi — not in mainland chicory varieties. Its two primary active compounds, cichoric acid and caftaric acid, are among the most potent antioxidant phenolic acids in the Mediterranean plant kingdom. These findings are from cell experiments and have not yet been confirmed in human trials.

Scientific analysis of the traditional Greek practice of boiling stamnagathi confirms that its water decoctions are rich in bioactive plant compounds — including cichoric acid, caftaric acid, and quercetin and luteolin glycosides — with strong antioxidant activity and no toxic effects on human cells. The study also identified sesquiterpene lactones, a class of plant compounds associated with anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective properties. These findings characterise stamnagathi's bioactive profile but have not yet been linked to specific clinical health outcomes in humans.

Research using a whole-organism model suggests that stamnagathi extract acts on fundamental cellular longevity pathways: when fed to Drosophila fruit flies — a well-validated model for studying ageing and cell biology — the extract altered the proteostasis network, the cellular system that clears damaged proteins and whose decline is a central driver of ageing, and caused widespread changes in lipid and amino acid metabolism. Distinct metabolic responses were observed between male and female flies, suggesting sex-specific interactions. These findings are from an invertebrate model and require validation in mammals and humans before clinical conclusions can be drawn.

Research from one of the largest dietary studies ever conducted — tracking over 521,000 people across 16 years — found that each extra tablespoon of olive oil per day was linked to a 4% lower risk of dying from heart disease or diabetes. Replacing butter or margarine with olive oil was associated with lower overall mortality, including from cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer, respiratory disease, and Alzheimer's disease. These are observational findings and cannot prove direct causation, but the exceptional scale and duration of this study make it among the strongest real-world evidence that olive oil is a meaningful contributor to a longer, healthier life.

A 6.5-year randomised trial from the PREDIMED programme found that people assigned to a Mediterranean diet enriched with extra virgin olive oil scored significantly higher on two standard cognitive tests — including a 0.62-point improvement on the Mini-Mental State Examination (p=0.005) and a 0.51-point improvement on the Clock Drawing Test (p=0.001) — compared to a low-fat control group. These differences held after adjusting for age, education, genetics, and cardiovascular risk factors. The likely drivers are EVOO's polyphenols, which cross the blood-brain barrier, reduce neuroinflammation, and protect neurons from oxidative damage. Note: EVOO was supplemented as part of a full Mediterranean diet — the effect cannot be attributed to olive oil alone.
